paragraphs: The paper presents a chip that assigns an incoming analog vector to one of several stored templates. This operation, called vector quantization, requires comparing the input with candidate representatives and choosing the closest one. The design performs these comparisons in parallel, making the selection process a direct operation of the analog circuitry.

Its core is a 16-by-16 array of charge-based distance cells that compares a 16-component input against 16 template vectors. Similarity is measured through mean absolute difference: the average magnitude of the componentwise discrepancies. Each cell includes dynamic template storage. A winner-take-all circuit then selects a single output, using global positive feedback to make that decision settle quickly and decisively.

Tests of the complete chip demonstrate correct operation with a 34-decibel analog input dynamic range, a 3-microsecond cycle time, and power consumption of 0.7 milliwatts. These measurements establish that the distance computation, template storage, and final selection work together in hardware. The contribution is a demonstrated parallel analog implementation of the full quantization operation.
neurips-1994-a-charge-based-cmos-paralle.tldr: A charge-based analog chip compares 16-component inputs with 16 templates in parallel and selects the closest match.

paragraphs: This paper models how the hippocampus could coordinate learning new patterns with recalling familiar ones. The network rapidly organizes representations of incoming signals and retrieves previously learned associations. Its central mechanism uses a comparison between incoming information and recalled information to regulate which kind of processing the network emphasizes.

The model assigns distinct roles to hippocampal regions. Input arrives through the perforant path, region CA3 recalls associations, and region CA1 compares that recall with the incoming signal. The comparison controls feedback affecting acetylcholine, a chemical modulator of neural activity. Novel patterns increase cholinergic modulation and favor storage of new representations; familiar patterns decrease it and favor retrieval using existing representations.

This arrangement connects recognition of novelty directly to the dynamics needed for learning. The proposed mechanism requires cholinergic suppression of synaptic transmission to be selective within particular parts of CA3 and CA1. The abstract states that this selectivity has experimental support. Thus, the model combines self-organization and associative memory through a specific feedback mechanism tied to a stated biological property.
neurips-1994-a-model-of-the-hippocampus-.tldr: A hippocampal model uses comparisons between incoming and recalled patterns to regulate acetylcholine and shift between learning and retrieval.

paragraphs: The paper implements a proposed explanation of schizophrenia in which degeneration of temporal-lobe projections triggers compensatory synaptic changes in connected brain regions. It focuses on the frontal cortex, representing it as an associative memory network. Connections carrying input into that network stand for the projections arriving from the temporal lobe.

The authors examine what happens when these external inputs weaken while internal connections strengthen and noise increases. In the model, those compensatory changes can preserve memory capacity. They also make stored memories emerge spontaneously and unevenly, so that some memories are retrieved more readily than others even without an external trigger.

The authors interpret this biased spontaneous retrieval as a model of hallucinations and delusions, including their concentration around a few recurring themes. They also use the model to explain declining symptoms as the illness progresses and slower responses following delayed intervention. These are explanations within the modeled theory. The central result is that changes preserving memory function can simultaneously produce abnormal retrieval, linking compensation and symptoms through one computational mechanism.
neurips-1994-a-neural-model-of-delusions.tldr: An associative-memory model links compensation for weakened inputs to preserved memory capacity and spontaneous, biased retrieval resembling psychotic symptoms.

paragraphs: The paper presents an electronic model of an axon, the part of a neuron that carries pulses. The intended role is as a building block for neural computations that depend on relationships among pulses across locations and times. For that purpose, the circuit needs to transmit pulses while preserving the features that make their timing meaningful.

The design reproduces several properties of its biological counterpart. It has a threshold for excitation and a brief refractory interval after a pulse, during which its response is restricted. It also restores both pulse amplitude and pulse width. These restoration mechanisms address two separate aspects of the signal: how strong the pulse is and how long it lasts.

The authors explain the circuit's operation and present measurements from a chip fabricated in a standard CMOS process. They particularly emphasize pulse-width restoration as necessary for stable propagation. This makes temporal shape a central engineering requirement: carrying a pulse reliably involves maintaining its duration as well as its amplitude. The hardware therefore addresses a concrete prerequisite for computations built around pulse correlations.
neurips-1994-a-silicon-axon-b428477cfc.tldr: A silicon axon preserves pulse amplitude and duration while reproducing excitation thresholds and refractory behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many simultaneous parameter perturbations should be used during a learning step. In the neural-network setting, the parameters are connection weights, and perturbative learning changes them to obtain information useful for improvement. The authors consider the number of parallel perturbations made each time a training pattern is presented.

Their new theoretical results favor a single parallel perturbation per pattern presentation in most cases. This gives a concrete answer to an implementation choice: repeatedly perturbing the parameters during the same presentation is not generally the theoretically preferred strategy. The finding refines their earlier work on parallel perturbative learning and its possible realization in analog integrated circuits.

The conclusion has explicit exceptions. Certain problems favor multiple perturbations, and hardware constraints such as limited numerical precision may also change the preferred choice. In those circumstances, the authors' earlier support for multiple perturbations still applies. The practical lesson is that the theoretical choice and the hardware choice depend on the conditions under which learning operates, with precision identified as one relevant constraint.
neurips-1994-a-study-of-parallel-perturb.tldr: One parallel perturbation per training pattern is usually theoretically preferred, but problem structure and limited hardware precision can favor several.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a learner should choose where to sample a function when its goal is to approximate that function accurately. It develops a Bayesian strategy for selecting observations according to their expected usefulness. The sampling decision becomes part of learning, with the objective of obtaining an accurate approximation from fewer examples.

The strategy draws on optimal experiment design and measures approximation quality using an objective that includes both bias and variance. Bias concerns systematic approximation error, while variance concerns how much the learned result can vary. Candidate observations are assessed by their potential contribution to improving this combined objective, connecting data selection directly to the quality of the eventual approximation.

The authors turn the general framework into explicit selection algorithms for unit step functions and polynomial functions. They then investigate whether these active choices reduce the number of examples needed to learn the target. Both theoretical and empirical results suggest that they can. The contribution combines a general principle for choosing informative samples with concrete applications to two specified function-learning problems.
neurips-1994-active-learning-for-functio.tldr: A Bayesian sampling strategy accounts for bias and variance to choose useful observations and potentially learn functions with fewer examples.

paragraphs: A mixture of experts combines several predictive components through a gating network that determines their contributions. This paper proposes a different parametric form for that gate. The change targets how the combined model is trained, making the design of the coordinating component central to the behavior of the overall learning system.

The modified model is trained with the expectation-maximization algorithm. According to the abstract, this formulation removes the need to choose a learning step size, a requirement in the earlier models considered by the authors. Simulation experiments show faster convergence. The reported advantage therefore concerns how efficiently training reaches a solution, alongside the elimination of a training parameter that would otherwise need selection.

The authors apply the architecture to two tasks: approximating piecewise nonlinear functions and combining classifiers that have already been trained. These applications use expert combination in different ways, either to represent parts of a function or to integrate existing predictors. Together they illustrate how changing the gate can support both learning a composite model and assembling one from previously learned components.
neurips-1994-an-alternative-model-for-mi.tldr: A revised gating model for mixtures of experts enables EM training without step-size selection and shows faster convergence in simulations.

paragraphs: The paper examines the long-run behavior of neural-network weights trained by gradient descent with a fixed learning constant and without batch processing. Its object of study is the sequence of weight estimates produced during training. The authors ask whether this sequence has a limiting statistical distribution and what properties that distribution has.

For the one-dimensional case, they provide an exact analysis establishing that a limiting distribution exists. That distribution need not be Gaussian, so a bell-shaped description is not generally justified. For the general case, the analysis assumes a small learning constant and uses a linear approximation. Results from random-matrix theory then establish a limiting distribution within that approximate treatment.

The authors examine the first few moments of the resulting distribution, quantities describing features such as its location and spread. They use these to compare their analysis with stochastic-approximation techniques. The contribution is a distributional account of long-run training behavior under a fixed learning constant, with a clear distinction between the exact one-dimensional result and the approximate analysis of the general setting.
neurips-1994-asymptotics-of-gradient-bas.tldr: Fixed-step gradient training can approach a limiting weight distribution that is not generally Gaussian.

paragraphs: When collecting observations is expensive, a learner benefits from choosing its next observation carefully. This paper develops a sequential query-selection method for neural-network models within Bayesian decision theory. Its distinguishing feature is that the value of a candidate observation depends explicitly on how the model's predictions will be used.

This connects data collection to the eventual prediction task. An observation is assessed through a criterion that incorporates the intended use of predictions, giving the selection process a purpose beyond simply accumulating more data. The quantities needed by the criterion are approximated using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, with the approximation carried out to a desired precision.

The framework also changes model complexity as the dataset grows, using Bayesian model selection. Data acquisition and model capacity are therefore both addressed within the learning process. Numerical experiments demonstrate properties of two versions of the query criterion. The contribution is a decision-based method for selecting informative observations while allowing the model's complexity to evolve with the available evidence.
neurips-1994-bayesian-query-construction.tldr: A Bayesian query strategy chooses new observations according to the intended use of predictions and adapts model complexity as data accumulates.

paragraphs: Radial basis function networks use locally responsive units, but many training methods require choosing the number of hidden units before learning begins. The paper builds on constructive methods that add units only when needed. These methods provide a growing architecture and, according to the abstract, reach training stability faster than gradient-descent approaches.

The specific starting point is P-RCE, which uses a single global setting for the spread of its prototypes. The proposed Dynamic Decay Adjustment algorithm retains the growing structure while adapting each prototype's decay factor independently. This factor controls how its response changes with distance. The adjustment also depends on class membership and distinguishes among different neighboring prototypes.

Giving each prototype its own decay setting lets the network tailor local responses instead of imposing one shared width throughout the model. The abstract reports substantially better performance than common radial basis function networks. The contribution brings together two forms of adaptation: deciding when additional units are needed and adjusting how broadly each existing unit responds to nearby inputs.
neurips-1994-boosting-the-performance-of.tldr: Dynamic Decay Adjustment improves growing RBF networks by adapting each prototype's response width using class-dependent neighborhood information.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to improve predictions of five-year breast cancer-specific survival. Its motivation is that the TNM staging framework cannot accommodate the expanding set of proposed prognostic factors. The authors describe a need for a computerized system that can assess those factors and combine useful predictors with the variables already used in staging.

They compare a broad set of approaches: pathological TNM staging, principal component analysis, classification and regression trees, logistic regression, and several neural-network methods. The neural approaches include cascade correlation, conjugate-gradient training, probabilistic networks, and backpropagation. Prediction accuracy is evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, placing the different approaches under a shared assessment criterion.

This comparison treats model choice as an empirical question about survival prediction and the integration of prognostic information. The supplied abstract cuts off during its results sentence, so it does not establish which methods outperform which alternatives. What it clearly provides is the clinical motivation, the prediction target, the candidate approaches, and the common evaluation framework.
neurips-1994-comparing-the-prediction-ac.tldr: The paper compares staging, statistical methods, and neural networks for five-year breast cancer survival prediction, but the supplied results sentence is incomplete.

paragraphs: The paper studies how the familiar K-means clustering algorithm converges. K-means represents data using cluster representatives and seeks to reduce quantization error, the error associated with that representation. The authors approach its behavior through optimization theory, asking what kind of mathematical update the clustering procedure actually performs.

They describe two existing ways to interpret the algorithm. One views it as gradient descent, connecting the updates to movement toward lower error. Another extends the mathematics of expectation-maximization to hard thresholding, where assignments select a cluster outright. These perspectives describe the same clustering procedure through different mathematical frameworks.

The paper's main claim is that K-means minimizes quantization error using Newton's method, which the abstract characterizes as very fast. This identifies a more specific optimization structure behind its updates and connects the convergence question to that structure. The contribution is an analysis of the established algorithm: understanding the method used to reduce its objective helps explain its behavior without requiring a newly proposed clustering procedure.
neurips-1994-convergence-properties-of-t.tldr: The paper interprets K-means as a Newton method for minimizing quantization error, clarifying its convergence behavior.

paragraphs: This paper describes a system that tracks facial expressions and uses them to control a simulated three-dimensional face in real time. It links visual analysis to facial motion through two neural-inspired operations: correlation and interpolation. The aim is to turn an observed facial state into the control signals needed to reproduce its expression.

A replicated correlation network computes a distributed, view-based representation of the face. Facial state is expressed through the combined responses of multiple view-correlation scores. Those scores then enter an interpolation network, which maps the perceptual representation to motor-control states. In the simulated face, the resulting activation levels correspond to muscles in an anatomically derived model.

The architecture connects fast two-dimensional image processing with a structured three-dimensional account of facial movement. Correlation supplies the visual description, and interpolation translates that description into coordinated muscle activations. The authors report that the integrated system can quickly track and interpret complex facial motions in real time, demonstrating a complete path from observed appearance to animated expression.
neurips-1994-correlation-and-interpolati.tldr: Correlation and interpolation networks translate observed facial expressions into muscle controls for a real-time three-dimensional face model.

paragraphs: The paper models direction selectivity in visual cortex while accounting for the large amount of excitation supplied by other cortical neurons. This anatomical motivation matters because the feedforward models described in the abstract place all excitation in incoming geniculate signals. The proposed circuit instead gives recurrent cortical excitation a major role in shaping responses.

The authors study a detailed model analytically and through biologically realistic simulations. It operates with hysteresis, meaning that its response depends on its activity history. Weak geniculate input is strongly amplified within the cortex. Inhibition both blocks early excitation for the nonpreferred direction and restrains excitation so neurons respond only while the stimulus occupies their receptive field.

The model explains several reported neuronal properties, including small changes in somatic input conductance during nonpreferred motion, differences between cortical and incoming velocity responses, and nonlinear contrast responses. It is compared with a classical model lacking recurrent excitation. The analysis also identifies limitations in grating-based tests of linearity and proposes hysteresis as a possible contributor to cortical function.
neurips-1994-direction-selectivity-in-pr.tldr: A recurrent cortical model combines strong excitation, inhibition, and hysteresis to explain multiple properties of direction-selective visual neurons.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the difficulty of understanding what a trained neural network has learned. Its goal is to turn network knowledge into compact if-then rules that people can inspect. This addresses a gap between successful prediction and human comprehension, especially when the network represents information through many interacting numerical values.

The proposed mechanism is validity interval analysis. The abstract describes it as a general tool that propagates rule-like knowledge through networks of the kind trained by backpropagation. By following such knowledge through the network, the method extracts symbolic statements from a representation that is originally numerical and distributed across units.

Empirical studies in a robot-arm domain illustrate the approach on networks with real-valued and distributed representations. That setting matters because a rule cannot simply be read off as the meaning of a single discrete unit. The reported studies support the suitability of the extraction method for these networks. The contribution is a concrete bridge from internal network computation to explicit conditional rules, making learned behavior more accessible to human interpretation.
neurips-1994-extracting-rules-from-artif.tldr: Validity interval analysis extracts readable if-then rules from neural networks with real-valued, distributed representations.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the proposal that the central nervous system uses an internal model to simulate the dynamics of the motor system. Such a model would represent how the system behaves over time and could contribute to movement planning, control, and learning. The abstract frames this proposal as previously motivated by computational principles without direct experimental validation.

The authors introduce an approach based on tracking how errors propagate through sensorimotor integration over time. Sensorimotor integration connects sensory information with the processes controlling movement. Examining the temporal progression of errors provides a way to investigate the internal computations involved, making their dynamics the focus of the experimental question.

The work combines experimental results with simulations, and the authors report direct support for an internal model. The significance is that the proposed mechanism is connected to observable error behavior through a specific investigative approach. The stated finding supports an internal simulation of motor dynamics as part of human motor processing, advancing the argument beyond its original computational motivation.
neurips-1994-forward-dynamic-models-in-h.tldr: Experiments and simulations tracking errors over time support the existence of an internal model of human motor dynamics.

paragraphs: Glove-TalkII converts hand gestures continuously into ten control parameters of a speech synthesizer. The hand acts as an artificial vocal tract, giving the user control over speech production, pitch, and volume in real time. Because the interface controls synthesis continuously, its vocabulary is not restricted to a predefined collection of words.

The system combines several input devices with three neural networks. A gating network weights the outputs of separate vowel and consonant networks. The gate and consonant network learn from examples provided by the user. The vowel network implements a fixed, user-defined relationship between hand position and vowel sound. Additional fixed mappings control volume, fundamental frequency, and stop consonants.

The abstract reports that one person learned to produce intelligible speech with the system. Speech was slow, with quality comparable to a text-to-speech synthesizer but substantially more natural pitch variation. This demonstrates a usable gesture-to-speech mapping for that participant while making the scope of the reported evidence clear. The system combines learned mappings and direct controls to support expressive, continuous speech production.
neurips-1994-glove-talkii-mapping-hand-g.tldr: Glove-TalkII uses neural networks and fixed controls to turn hand gestures into continuous speech, demonstrated intelligibly by one trained user.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people improve at judging motion direction when the visual stimulus contains randomness. The authors report psychophysical experiments demonstrating perceptual learning for this task. They describe perceptual learning as a rapid performance improvement whose benefit persists over time, making retained improvement the behavior that their models seek to explain.

They investigate two ways learning might handle the motion noise. A clustering model learns to accommodate it, whereas an averaging model learns to ignore it. This distinction concerns what changes during learning: the models take different approaches to the same noisy evidence while aiming to improve the direction judgment.

Simulations of both models produce performance similar to the psychophysical results. The reported agreement shows that the observed learning is compatible with two different computational treatments of noise. It therefore connects a behavioral finding to explicit candidate mechanisms without identifying a single mechanism as the sole explanation. The contribution is the joint experimental and modeling account of how motion discrimination can improve through learning.
neurips-1994-learning-direction-in-globa.tldr: Clustering and averaging models both reproduce aspects of perceptual learning in noisy motion-direction judgments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for calculating a response function and its average for linear perceptrons. These quantities provide access to much of the behavior of learning and generalization. The main question is how theoretical results for infinitely large systems relate to networks with a finite number of parameters.

The authors first recover known results in the thermodynamic limit, where perceptron size grows without bound. They explicitly show that the response function becomes self-averaging: variation between individual instances loses importance in that limit. They also discuss extensions to settings with direction-dependent assumptions about target weights, different input distributions, and weight-decay terms.

The method then calculates corrections to the average response that scale as the inverse of network size. These corrections allow the authors to examine how finite size affects prediction on new examples and the course of learning. Their stated conclusion is that infinite-size results can often be relevant even for fairly modest systems. The finite-size analysis supplies the connection between the mathematical limit and that practical relevance.
neurips-1994-learning-in-large-linear-pe.tldr: A response-function analysis shows why infinite-size learning results can remain relevant to linear perceptrons of modest size.

paragraphs: The paper presents a framework for learning saccades, the rapid eye movements used to redirect gaze. It represents target locations in natural scenes through their visual appearance. Each target is described by a high-dimensional vector of spatial-filter responses, with filters operating at different orientations and scales.

The first demonstration uses this representation to locate points that were previously foveated, meaning they had earlier been brought to the center of gaze. Recovering those points gives the framework a way to identify a previously viewed target within the scene. The combination of filter scales and orientations supplies the appearance information used for this localization.

The authors then incorporate that capability into a strategy involving multiple saccades. This strategy derives an adaptive motor map for producing accurate gaze shifts. The contribution connects a perceptual task, recognizing where a target is, with a motor-learning task, determining how to move the eyes toward it. The same visual representation provides the link between returning to a known scene point and learning accurate movement.
neurips-1994-learning-saccadic-eye-movem.tldr: Multiscale visual-filter responses help relocate previously viewed targets and learn a motor map for accurate eye movements.

paragraphs: The paper examines committees of neural networks for learning functions with continuous-valued outputs. It connects three uses of such ensembles: improving prediction accuracy, estimating error on new examples, and choosing additional training data. The common quantity is ambiguity, defined as the variation among network outputs averaged over unlabeled inputs.

Ambiguity measures how much the members disagree without requiring correct answers for those inputs. The authors explain how to combine it with cross-validation to obtain a reliable estimate of ensemble generalization error. They also discuss cases where this ensemble form of cross-validation improves performance, and show how unlabeled data can help estimate optimal weights for combining the members.

The same disagreement measure supports active learning through an extension of query by committee. It helps select new examples whose labels should be acquired. Thus, unlabeled inputs contribute both to understanding the current ensemble and to deciding how to improve it. The paper's central connection is that variation among predictors can inform evaluation, combination, and future data collection within one framework.
neurips-1994-neural-network-ensembles-cr.tldr: Disagreement among neural networks helps estimate ensemble error, choose combination weights, and select new examples for labeling.

paragraphs: The paper studies binary classification when each training example is presented only once. In this online setting, the number of examples also measures learning time. The authors analyze how error on unseen examples declines and show that the schedule for reducing the learning rate is central to that decline.

When the target rule can be represented by a perceptron, an optimized schedule can make error decrease as fast as the inverse of the number of examples. When the target cannot be represented, the ordinary perceptron algorithm need not reach the lowest achievable generalization error. For a particular case involving simple output noise, the authors propose an algorithm whose error can approach the optimum at an inverse-square-root rate.

They also extend the perceptron algorithm to classes of smooth functions converted into binary decisions by thresholding. For suitable input distributions, inverse-example error decay is possible if the algorithm converges to the optimal solution. That convergence condition is explicit. The results distinguish learning speed from the separate question of whether an algorithm reaches the best available predictor.
neurips-1994-on-line-learning-of-dichoto.tldr: Online classification rates depend on learning-rate schedules and target representability, with a modified perceptron handling a specified output-noise case.

paragraphs: The paper develops an analytical framework for estimating how localized structural damage affects a neural network's function. It studies a spatially organized associative memory, where function is assessed through the capacity to retrieve stored information. The motivating question is how the geometry and distribution of damage relate to the resulting memory impairment.

The analysis varies lesion area, shape, and number. This makes the pattern of damage part of the explanation, allowing several aspects of a lesion configuration to be examined together. Although the mathematical results rely on approximations, the abstract reports good agreement with simulations. That agreement supports the framework as a way to estimate retrieval damage in the modeled network.

The authors connect the results to features of multi-infarct dementia, particularly the association between infarct count and dementia after stroke. They also discuss a proposed multiplicative interaction between Alzheimer's disease and multi-infarct dementia. These connections give the computational study its clinical motivation: a model of localized damage can help interpret how different patterns of injury relate to functional loss.
neurips-1994-patterns-of-damage-in-neura.tldr: An associative-memory analysis links lesion area, shape, and number to retrieval damage, with approximate predictions supported by simulations.

paragraphs: Competitive learning needs a way for network units to develop different roles. The paper describes a difficulty with achieving this through neural activity: simple inhibition supports sparse representations, while decorrelation and factorization approaches supporting distributed representations are computationally unattractive. The authors seek competition compatible with information being represented across many units.

Their proposal places the competitive interaction in neural plasticity, the processes that change connections during learning. This shifts the mechanism responsible for differentiation toward how units learn. The abstract describes the resulting alternatives as diffuse and nonadaptive, and states that they support fully distributed representations. The distinction matters because differentiation need not depend on limiting activity to a small subset of units.

The authors apply the technique to their binary information-gain optimization algorithm for feature extraction, reporting that it simplifies and improves the method. They also propose that the approach could benefit other learning algorithms. The demonstrated contribution is the feature-extraction application; the broader idea is to use interactions in learning itself to organize distinct roles within a distributed representation.
neurips-1994-plasticity-mediated-competi.tldr: Mediating competition through plasticity supports distributed representations and simplifies an information-gain feature-learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Speech recognizers can perform poorly for people whose voices differ from those represented in training. This paper explores enlarging speaker diversity by transforming existing recordings. The motivation is to address variation among speakers without relying entirely on the expensive process of collecting speech from additional people.

The authors apply simple linear spectral warping to a 48-talker training database used for word spotting. This transformation modifies spectral properties of the recorded speech to create additional training-talker variants. The abstract compares the idea to warping handwritten-digit images, while emphasizing that speech varies along many dimensions, including linguistic content, pronunciation, timing, style, and spectral characteristics.

Average detection rates rise from 68.3% to 71.2% for male speakers and from 64.8% to 67.3% for female speakers. These are gains of 2.9 and 2.5 percentage points, respectively. The authors describe the improvement as small but comparable to doubling the amount of training data. The result supports transformed recordings as a useful way to increase effective training diversity for the tested word-spotting system.
neurips-1994-using-voice-transformations.tldr: Spectrally transformed training voices improve word-spotting detection by amounts comparable to doubling the training data.
